overview: French Somaliland was a French colonial territory around Djibouti and the Gulf of Tadjoura, not the whole Somali-speaking region or today’s Somaliland administration. The territory took the name French Somali Coast in 1896. This imported record covers only 1938 to 1945, a slice of a much longer colonial history; the endpoint does not mark independence.

periods.title: A colony before the war
periods.summary: French colonial officials regulated prices and services in a territory already established decades earlier.

periods.title: Vichy rule and wartime hardship
periods.summary: Vichy control, British blockade and political repression shaped the war years; the colony passed to Free French control at the end of 1942.

periods.title: Free French administration
periods.summary: New authorities reorganized the militia and its pay, equipment and medical deductions while colonial rule continued.

items.text: A wooden Issa milk vessel in the British Museum dates to around 1930 to 1934, just before this map window. Collected at Rahale, it has carved side handles threaded with twisted fibre cord. The collector recorded its use for milking. Its carefully shaped body brings household work into a history often dominated by ports and governors.

A July 1938 price-control order covered everyday purchases including salt, sugar and roasted coffee. Increases in wholesale and retail prices for listed goods needed authorization. The committee was instructed to consider import-price changes and prices paid to local producers, showing how distant markets could enter local shopping disputes.

The same order reached well beyond food: soap, children’s clothing, fishing nets, shoe repairs, laundry, water and electricity all appeared in its categories. Even repairing a worn shoe had a place in the official paperwork. These were regulated categories, not a shopping list every family could afford.

A school-inspection order issued in January 1941 distinguished public schools from private ones. It assigned public-school oversight to the education service and allowed a designated public teacher to inspect rural schools. The document reveals a network with different kinds of classrooms and supervision during wartime.

An attested French phrase from the 1938 order is “Côte française des Somalis,” meaning “French Somali Coast.” It appears in the governor’s formal title. This is the colonial administration’s written language and territorial name; it does not stand in for the languages spoken in local households.

The militia regulations of February 1943 provided monthly pay and daily food rations, including rations for camel guides and herders. Camels could receive grain when needed. A patrol depended on feeding the people who handled its animals as well as on feeding the animals themselves.

The prescribed camp kit included cooking pots, canvas buckets and mosquito nets. Camel units were assigned large metal barrels for transporting water, while personal equipment included water containers and eating utensils. The equipment list makes a simple point: staying supplied was part of the work, even when nobody was fighting.

Hospital treatment could cut a militiaman’s income. Under the 1943 rules, admission normally brought a deduction of one-third of net pay and loss of the daily ration. A wound received on assigned duty exempted him from the pay deduction. Medical care and household finances were closely connected.

sections.title: A world war at the dinner table

items.text: British efforts to isolate the colony reached livestock markets. The British administrative history describes cooperation with the Sultan of Aussa and purchases of goats and cattle intended to divert food away from French Somaliland. When cash did not attract enough interest, officials offered cloth in the same markets.

The sea was harder to seal. That British account says dhow traffic between the Gulf of Tadjoura and Arabia could not be controlled with the ships available, and records the blockade’s lifting on 24 March 1942. Small trading vessels complicate the picture of a perfectly closed wartime frontier.

War also brought severe hunger and repression. Governor Pierre Nouailhetas punished people suspected of helping the Allies with confinement, forced labor and executions. The Air Force historical guide describes famine under the blockade and some relief as imports resumed after the late-1942 transfer to Free French authorities.

A change of rulers could reach directly into a purse. Economist Richard Lester reported that the Free French required an exchange of Djibouti banknotes in January 1943. Larger registered holdings received proportionately less new money because a progressive levy accompanied the exchange. The paper people used to buy things became part of wartime policy.

ending.text: Colonial rule continued beyond the map’s 1945 endpoint. The territory was renamed the French Territory of the Afars and Issas in 1967; in 1977 it became the independent Republic of Djibouti. A change of official name did not erase the communities living there.
